title: Read an abstract for its main idea
objective: Find the purpose, one important detail and the main result.

slides.title: Read twice with two jobs
body: Skim: read quickly to find the main question.
Scan: look for one detail, such as a time or number.
An introduction explains why the question matters. An abstract gives a short account of the whole study.

slides.title: Try a short practice abstract
body: A class asked where ants were seen. At noon, students counted 7 ants by a tree and 2 by a wall.
Main idea: The class compared ant counts in two places.
One detail: The students counted at noon. Which sentence answers “Where?”

slides.title: Read the first case together
body: Practice abstract: We asked when birds visit a garden. We watched for ten minutes in the morning and ten in the afternoon. We saw eight birds in the morning and three in the afternoon.

slides.title: Try it with a partner
body: What question did the team ask?
Find the time spent watching and both counts.

slides.title: Try a new case
body: Practice abstract: We asked when bees visit flowers. We watched for ten minutes in the morning and ten in the afternoon. We saw four bees in the morning and nine in the afternoon.

slides.title: Work on your own
body: What question did the team ask?
Find the time spent watching and both counts.
Write the main finding in one clear sentence.

slides.title: Write one careful result
body: Use one complete sentence. Keep the time or place if it changes what the result means.
